title: Good Places to Live and Sleep Well: A Literature Review about the Role of Architecture in Determining Non-Visual Effects of Light
review_question: To deepen the complex issue of the interaction mechanism between light and architecture, specifically reviewing available research works about the role of architecture in determining non-visual effects of light.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Scopus search for engineering papers using keywords: circadian light, human centric lighting, integrative lighting, non-image-forming effects of light, non-visual effects of light, circadian stimulus, equivalent melanopic. Excluded: general reviews, papers on calculation methods, visual responses only, or light source characteristics only (not interacting with architectural elements).

evidence_base_summary.date_range: Not specified for search, cited papers range from 2000-2020

findings.antecedent: Urban design factors (building location, dimensions, shape, orientation, mutual position, green areas)
findings.consequent: Daylight characteristics (amount of light, hours of irradiation, spectral composition)
findings.quote: all these factors strongly affect daylight characteristics inside buildings, determining both the amount of light entering the spaces and the number of hours during which façades are irradiated

findings.antecedent: Architectural design (planimetric distribution, window shape/dimensions, window typology)
findings.consequent: Indoor daylight characteristics (amount, distribution, spectral composition)
findings.quote: choices like the planimetric distribution of the spaces and the shape and dimensions of windows define both the amount of indoor daylight and its distribution

findings.antecedent: Technological choices (opaque/transparent materials, building envelope configuration, visual transmittance, shading systems, non-neutral/colored glass, redirecting systems, light tubes)
findings.quote: The configuration of the building envelope affects the amount of daylight... the spectrum... and the indoor distribution

findings.antecedent: Interior design choices (wall color/reflectance, colored surfaces, furniture location, workstation positioning)
findings.consequent: Indoor light characteristics (light levels, spectrum, luminance distribution in visual field), circadian effects
findings.quote: interior design choices have an impact on circadian effects as well since they modify characteristics of both daylight and electric light.

findings.antecedent: Window orientation and typology (side-lit vs. skylights), direction of view
findings.quote: the CNVE mostly depends on the orientation and typology of the window and on the direction of view.

findings.consequent: CNVE for specific time ranges (6:00–10:00 vs. 10:00–18:00)
findings.quote: the orientation optimizing the CNVE in the range 6:00–10:00... is east and that optimizing the CNVE in the range 10-00–18:00 is south.

findings.antecedent: Distance from window, wall paint color
findings.quote: the variables most affecting the circadian stimulation were distance from the window and wall paint color.

findings.antecedent: Window-to-façade ratio, bed location (close to window vs. center), room surface reflectance, city (London vs. Madrid)
findings.quote: In London, to guarantee a proper CS entrainment... a window-to-façade ratio of 30% is necessary if the bed is close to the window, and of at least 60% if it is in the center of the room.

findings.antecedent: Surface reflectance (low reflectance vs. white work plane vs. pale blue desk), window size (large vs. small opening)
findings.quote: the presence of low reflectance surfaces strictly reduces the CS. A white work plane allows an increase in CS of up to 30% compared to a pale blue desk

findings.antecedent: Environment reflectance, typical weather conditions, latitude
findings.quote: the environment reflectance is one of the most influential variables, just as the typical weather conditions are more decisive than latitude in promoting a good CS.

findings.antecedent: Interior wall color (yellow, blue, gray vs. white), observer's distance from window, observer's view direction (towards wall vs. window)
findings.quote: all three of the colors determine lower CS values compared to the reference case. The worst results were obtained with yellow, followed by blue and gray.
the use of the different indoor colors determines a reduction in the CS values equal to 6%, 9% and 12% for the red, orange and yellow cases, respectively.

findings.consequent: Spectral reflectance of light at eye level (30% from reflections)
findings.quote: the component of the light incident at the observer's eye level directly emitted by the luminaire is equal to about 70%... and the remaining 30% is due to surface reflections.

findings.antecedent: Interior wall color (red vs. blue), CCT (6300K LED)
findings.quote: the use of red for the walls causes a reduction of the CAF equal to 1.3% and to 2.5%... whereas the use of blue for the walls causes an increase in the CAF equal to 8.4% and to 6.9%.

findings.antecedent: Glazing type (dark blue vs. other types)
findings.quote: the dark blue glazing causes very low CS values (< 0.3) across all times in comparison to other glazing types

findings.antecedent: Glazing type (low-e, high visual transmittance vs. bronze-tinted solar protective), Interior wall color (blue vs. orange), Material properties (spectrally neutral vs. non-neutral, transmissivity/reflectance)
findings.quote: low-e glazing with high visual transmittance and blue walls are the combinations with the highest non-visual entrainment, while the opposite is true for the combination of bronze-tinted solar protective glazing and orange walls.

findings.antecedent: Fiber optic daylighting system (FODS) layout (10, 24, 40 devices), horizontal illuminance
findings.consequent: Circadian Stimulus (CS), homogeneity of CS across positions
findings.quote: the percentage of observed CS values is higher than 0.3 for less than 20% with layout 1, 40% with layout 2 and achieves around 60% with layout 3.

synthesis_conclusions: Architectural design plays a fundamental role in defining the quantity and quality of light received by people, impacting non-visual effects and circadian systems.
Evaluating the mutual interactions between light and architecture for circadian effects is complex, making comparisons across studies difficult due to diverse methodologies.
It is currently challenging to quantify the precise weight of each architectural factor in modifying light characteristics and subsequent circadian effects.

Solutions for maximizing non-visual comfort often align with those for visual comfort, including optimal building position, window-to-wall ratio, maximizing daylight, and using highly reflective, neutral materials.
An integrative lighting culture is necessary to design spaces that promote well-being and sleep quality by considering all aspects of lighting synergistically.
evidence_gaps: Lack of shared and clear methods to evaluate lighting effects on circadian rhythm regulation.
Coexistence of multiple, non-comparable metrics for defining the circadian effect of light.
Absence of defined limit thresholds for evaluation parameters, especially considering the timing-dependent nature of circadian lighting.
Need for a spectrally based analysis approach for non-visual conditions, moving beyond traditional photopic illuminance patterns.
Scarce availability and widespread use of calculation software capable of spectrally based evaluation of light, including inter-reflections and dynamic conditions.
Difficulty in accurately modeling and collecting spectral data for daylight sources, which continuously change based on time, weather, season, and location.

Challenges in performing field measurements for architectural parameters' effects on circadian stimulation due to cost, instrument availability, and the onerous nature of repeated measurements for natural variations.
limitations: Difficulty in comparing results across studies due to differing methodological approaches and lack of shared evaluation techniques.
Inability to precisely quantify the weight of individual architectural factors on light characteristics and circadian effects.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Light plays a crucial role in affecting the melatonin secretion process, and consequently the sleep–wake cycle. Research has demonstrated that the main characteristics of lighting affecting the so-called circadian rhythms are spectrum, light levels, spatial pattern and temporal pattern (i.e., duration of exposure, timing and previous exposure history). Considering that today people spend most of their time in indoor environments, the light dose they receive strictly depends on the characteristics of the spaces where they live: location and orientation of the building, dimensions of the windows, presence of external obstructions, geometric characteristics of the space, optical properties of walls and furniture. Understanding the interaction mechanism between light and architecture is fundamental to design non-visually comfortable spaces. The goal of the paper is to deepen this complex issue. It is divided into two parts: a brief historical excursus about the relationship between lighting practice and architecture throughout the centuries and a review of the available research works about the topic. The analysis demonstrates that despite the efforts of the research, numerous open questions still remain, and they are mostly due to the lack of a shared and clear method to evaluate the effects of lighting on circadian rhythm regulation.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Light exposure, particularly to specific wavelengths and intensities, influences human physiology and behavior through non-visual pathways, primarily via intrinsically photosensitive Retinal Ganglion Cells (ipRGCs) and the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), affecting circadian rhythms, sleep, and alertness.

mechanism_chain.description: Architectural and urban design factors influence daylight characteristics, which in turn activate non-visual photoreceptors in the eye, transmitting signals to the brain's master clock (SCN) to regulate circadian rhythms and melatonin secretion, ultimately impacting sleep and overall well-being.
